Section. Introduction. The completeness theorem is one of the most fundamental results about logic. It comes in two formulations the equivalence of which we'll prove. In its first formulation it says something fundamental about the relationship between semantic consequence and our derivation system if a sentence Mathematical expression. A. End mathematical expression. follows from some sentences Mathematical expression. Gamma. End mathematical expression. then there is also a derivation that establishes Mathematical expression. Gamma syntactically derives A. End mathematical expression. Thus the derivation system is as strong as it can possibly be without proving things that don't actually follow. In its second formulation it can be stated as a model existence result every consistent set of sentences is satisfiable. Consistency is a proof-theoretic notion it says that our derivation system is unable to produce certain derivations. But who's to say that just because there are no derivations of a certain sort from Mathematical expression. Gamma. End mathematical expression. it's guaranteed that there is a structure Mathematical expression. structure M. End mathematical expression? Before the completeness theorem was first proved in fact before we had the derivation systems we now do the great German mathematician David Hilbert held the view that consistency of mathematical theories guarantees the existence of the objects they are about. He put it as follows in a letter to Gottlob Frege Begin quote. If the arbitrarily given axioms do not contradict one another with all their consequences then they are true and the things defined by the axioms exist. This is for me the criterion of truth and existence. Frege vehemently disagreed. The second formulation of the completeness theorem shows that Hilbert was right in at least the sense that if the axioms are consistent then some structure exists that makes them all true. These aren't the only reasons the completeness theorem or rather its proof is important. It has a number of important consequences some of which we'll discuss separately. For instance since any derivation that shows Mathematical expression. Gamma syntactically derives A. End mathematical expression. is finite and so can only use finitely many of the sentences in Mathematical expression. Gamma. End mathematical expression. it follows by the completeness theorem that if Mathematical expression. A. End mathematical expression. is a consequence of Mathematical expression. Gamma. End mathematical expression. it is already a consequence of a finite subset of Mathematical expression. Gamma. End mathematical expression. This is called compactness. Equivalently if every finite subset of Mathematical expression. Gamma. End mathematical expression. is consistent then Mathematical expression. Gamma. End mathematical expression. itself must be consistent. Although the compactness theorem follows from the completeness theorem via the detour through derivations it is also possible to use the the proof of the completeness theorem to establish it directly. For what the proof does is take a set of sentences with a certain property consistency and constructs a structure out of this set that has certain properties in this case that it satisfies the set. Almost the very same construction can be used to directly establish compactness by starting from finitely satisfiable sets of sentences instead of consistent ones. The construction also yields other consequences e.g. that any satisfiable set of sentences has a finite or denumerables model. This result is called the Lowenheim Skolem theorem. In general the construction of structures from sets of sentences is used often in logic and sometimes even in philosophy. End chapter.
